cards.explanation: The answer is that the emperor Claudius ordered all Jews out. Aquila and Priscilla had just come from Italy because Claudius, the Roman emperor, had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Nobody packs for a move like that on a whim, friends. I once got moved out of a kitchen drawer, so I know a little about being sent somewhere you didn't plan.

The answer is that they're tentmakers by trade, like Paul. The text says Aquila and Priscilla were tentmakers by trade, just as Paul was. Same trade, so staying and working with them made sense. When I find somebody else who loves a good rolling pin, I'm there all day too, friends.
The answer is False. The text says Paul was trying to persuade Jews and Greeks alike, every Sabbath. So the synagogue crowd wasn't only Jews, friends. Paul was talking to both groups.
The answer is the Christ. Paul was testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ, friends. Once Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, he devoted himself fully to the word.
The answer is the Gentiles. Paul told them, “From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” Gentiles are people who aren't Jews, friends. The insults at the synagogue were the moment he said it.

The answer is the house of Titus Justus next door. Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God. He didn't have far to walk, friends. I think that was a pretty short commute for such a big change.

The answer is True. Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord. The man in charge of the synagogue, and his whole household with him! Paul had left that synagogue after being opposed and insulted (Acts 18:6), and still its leader believed. I'd have needed to sit down, friends.

The answer is baptized. Many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized. Hearing, believing, baptism: the verse lays it out in that order, friends. That's a lot of people packed into one sentence.

The answer is afraid. The Lord told Paul in a vision, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent.” Three short commands, back to back, friends. I think a man who'd just been opposed and insulted could use all three.

The answer is that He has many people in this city. The Lord said, “For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city.” Two promises in one line, friends: He is with Paul, and no one will lay a hand on him. The reason He gives is that He has many people in this city.

The answer is a year and a half. Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians. That's a long stretch in one place, friends. I've spent longer than that stuck in the back of a junk drawer, so I know a long stay.

The answer is before the judgment seat. The Jews coordinated an attack on Paul and brought him before the judgment seat. This happened while Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, a Roman official over that region, friends. It was a big step from arguing in a synagogue.

The answer is False. Just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio, the proconsul, spoke to the Jews instead. The text gives no defense from Paul in that scene, friends. I think that was a strange moment, being ready to talk and then not needed.

The answer is a dispute about words and their own law. Gallio told the Jews, “But since it is a dispute about words and names and your own law, settle it yourselves.” He's saying it isn't a wrongdoing or vicious crime, friends. To him, it was a matter for them to sort out.

The answer is True. Gallio said, “…settle it yourselves.” Then he added, “I refuse to be a judge of such things.” He was the proconsul sitting at the judgment seat, friends, and he still handed it back.

The answer is False. This part is heavy, friends. The crowd seized Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him in front of the judgment seat. The text says, “But none of this was of concern to Gallio.” I think it's a hard thing to read, and Paul's story isn't over yet.
